A strip of paper with parallel edges $3$ cm apart is folded so that part of it partially overlaps the rest of the strip (see figure). What is the minimum possible area of the shaded region?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_1997_p1_fig.png

Let $f$ be a real function of a real variable satisfying
$$\text{(i)}\ f(10 + x) = f(10 - x), \qquad \text{(ii)}\ f(20 + x) = -f(20 - x)$$
for every real $x$. Prove that $f$ is odd and periodic.

(Recall that $f$ is odd if $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for every $x$, and periodic if there is $T > 0$ such that $f(x + T) = f(x)$ for every $x$.)

Consider the infinite quadrant in the figure, in which all small squares have side $1$. Is it possible to colour some of the small squares black so that both of the following properties hold?

• For every positive integer $n$, the square with a vertex at $O$ and side $n$ (with sides parallel to the axes) contains more black squares than white squares.

• Every infinite diagonal of small squares parallel to the one shown in the figure contains at most finitely many black squares.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_1997_p3_fig.png

Let $ABCD$ be an arbitrary tetrahedron. The length $a$ of the edge $AB$ is known, as well as the area $S$ of the projection of the tetrahedron onto a plane perpendicular to the line $AB$. Determine the volume of the tetrahedron.

Let $X$ be the set of positive integers whose decimal representation does not consist of a single digit repeated. For every $n \in X$, let $A_n$ be the set of numbers obtained by permuting the digits of $n$ in all possible ways, and let $d_n$ be the greatest common divisor of all numbers in $A_n$. For example, if $n = 1120$, then
$$A_{1120} = \{112, 121, 211, 1012, 1021, 1102, 1120, 1201, 1210, 2011, 2101, 2110\}$$
and $d_{1120} = 1$ (since $112$ and $121$ are relatively prime). Find the largest possible value of $d_n$.

A travelling salesman must plan a trip that lets him visit all the cities shown in the diagram, starting from $A$ and returning to $A$. Solid lines represent railway connections between cities and dashed lines represent air connections. A train ticket between two directly connected cities costs $150\,000$ lire, while a plane ticket costs $250\,000$ lire. What is the minimum amount the salesman must spend?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_1997_p6_fig.png

For a positive real number $x$, let $[x]$ denote the integer part of $x$, i.e. the largest integer $n \le x$. Compute the sum
$$\sum_{n=1}^{1\,000\,000} \left[\sqrt{n}\right] = \left[\sqrt{1}\right] + \left[\sqrt{2}\right] + \cdots + \left[\sqrt{999\,999}\right] + \left[\sqrt{1\,000\,000}\right].$$
(You may use, without proof, the formula $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} i^2 = \frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}$.)
Prove that every convex polyhedron has at least two faces with the same number of sides.

Alberto wants to organise a game of poker for this evening. He knows that Bruno and Barbara go to the gym together one evening out of three, and that Carla, Corrado, Dario and Davide are each busy one evening out of two (not necessarily on the same days). He also knows that Dario refuses to play with Davide, since Davide stole his girlfriend. Since at least four people (including Alberto) are needed to play poker, what is the probability that the game takes place this evening?

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with longer base $AB$ whose diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ and let $E$ be the intersection of the lines $OB$ and $CD$. Prove that
$$BC^2 = CD \cdot CE.$$

Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$ be four distinct integers and let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that
$$P(a_1) = P(a_2) = P(a_3) = P(a_4) = 1. \qquad (*)$$

(i) Prove that there is no integer $n$ with $P(n) = 12$.

(ii) Do there exist a polynomial $P(x)$ satisfying $(*)$ and an integer $n$ with $P(n) = 1998$?

Let $f$ be a function defined on the positive integers and taking positive integer values. We say that $f$ is increasing if $n < m$ implies $f(n) < f(m)$; multiplicative if $\gcd(m, n) = 1$ implies $f(nm) = f(n)f(m)$; completely multiplicative if $f(nm) = f(n)f(m)$ for all $n$, $m$.

(i) Prove that if $f$ is increasing, then $f(n) \ge n$ for every $n$.

(ii) Prove that if $f$ is increasing, completely multiplicative and $f(2) = 2$, then $f(n) = n$ for every $n$.

(iii) Does statement (ii) remain true if the word completely is removed?

A rectangular sheet of paper has sides $a$ and $b$ with $a > b$. It is folded along a diagonal. Determine the area of the triangle formed by the overlap of the two flaps (the grey triangle in the figure).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_1999_p1_fig.png

A positive integer is called balanced if it has as many digits as it has distinct prime divisors (for example, $15$ is balanced, while $49$ is not). Prove that there are only finitely many balanced numbers.

Let $\Gamma$, $\Gamma_1$, $\Gamma_2$ be three circles with radii $r$, $r_1$, $r_2$ respectively, where $0 < r_1 < r_2 < r$. The circles $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ are internally tangent to $\Gamma$ at two distinct points $A$ and $B$, and they meet each other at two distinct points. Prove that the segment $AB$ passes through one of the intersection points of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ if and only if $r_1 + r_2 = r$.

Alberto and Barbara play the following game. There are $1999$ matches on a table. In turn, each player must remove from the table a number of matches of their choice, which must be at least $1$ and at most half of the number of matches on the table at that moment. The player who leaves a single match on the table loses. Barbara moves first. Determine which of the two players has a winning strategy and describe that strategy.

On a lake there is a village of huts built on stilts at the nodes of an $m \times n$ rectangular grid (for example, a grid of $3$ rows of $5$ huts). Exactly $p$ bridges leave the platform of each hut, connecting it to one or more neighbouring huts (neighbouring in the grid, so not diagonally). For which positive integers $m$, $n$, $p$ is it possible to place the bridges so that every hut can be reached from every other hut? (Of course, several bridges may be placed between two neighbouring huts.)

(a) Find all pairs $(x, k)$ of positive integers satisfying
$$3^k - 1 = x^3.$$

(b) Prove that if $n > 1$ is an integer different from $3$, there are no pairs $(x, k)$ of positive integers satisfying
$$3^k - 1 = x^n.$$

Three odd numbers $a < b < c$ are called consecutive if $c - b = b - a = 2$. An integer is called special if all its digits are equal and it can be written as the sum of the squares of three consecutive odd numbers.

(a) Find all special numbers with $4$ digits.

(b) Are there special numbers with $2000$ digits?

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, and let $\angle DAB = \alpha$, $\angle ADB = \beta$, $\angle ACB = \gamma$, $\angle DBC = \delta$, $\angle DBA = \varepsilon$. Given that $\alpha < 90^\circ$, $\beta + \gamma = 90^\circ$ and $\delta + 2\varepsilon = 180^\circ$, prove that
$$(DB + BC)^2 = AD^2 + AC^2.$$

A pyramid with base a quadrilateral $ABCD$ and apex $V$ is inscribed in a sphere. It is known that $AD = 2BC$ and that the lines $AB$ and $CD$, extended, meet at a point $E$ on the same side as the segment $BC$. Compute the ratio of the volume of the pyramid with base triangle $AED$ and apex $V$ to the volume of the given pyramid.

Fix an integer $n > 1$. Alberto and Barbara play the following game:

1. Alberto chooses a positive integer.

2. Barbara chooses an integer greater than $1$ that is a multiple or a divisor of Alberto's number (possibly the number itself).

3. Alberto gives Barbara back the number she said, possibly adding or subtracting $1$.

The game continues by alternately repeating steps 2 and 3. Barbara wins if she manages to choose $n$ within $50$ moves. For which values of $n$ can Barbara win against every strategy of Alberto?

A welder has metal rods of length $2$ and wants to build a grid consisting of $n \times n$ small squares of side $1$ (a $5 \times 5$ example is shown in the figure). He is allowed to cut rods in half and to weld rods together, but without overlapping or crossing them. What is the minimum number of rods that must be cut in half to build the grid?

In the figure, below the grid: on the left, examples of allowed configurations; on the right, examples of forbidden configurations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2000_p5_fig.png

Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(0) = 0$ and $0 \le p(1) \le 10^7$. Given that there are two positive integers $a$, $b$ with $p(a) = 1999$ and $p(b) = 2001$, determine the possible values of $p(1)$. (Note that $1999$ is a prime.)
In a hexagon with all angles equal, four consecutive sides have lengths $5$, $3$, $6$ and $7$ (in this order). Find the lengths of the remaining two sides.

In a basketball tournament every team plays twice against every other team. A single team wins the tournament with $26$ points, and exactly two teams finish in last place with $20$ points. How many teams took part in the tournament? (A win gives $2$ points, a loss $0$ points, and no game can end in a draw.)

Consider the equation $x^{2001} = y^x$.

(a) Find all pairs $(x, y)$ of solutions with $x$ a prime and $y$ a positive integer.

(b) Find all pairs $(x, y)$ of positive integers satisfying the equation.

(Recall that $2001 = 3 \cdot 23 \cdot 29$.)

A positive integer is called monotone if its decimal representation

• has at least two digits,

• has all digits different from zero,

• has its digits in strictly increasing or strictly decreasing order.

(For example, $127$ and $9742$ are monotone, whereas $172$, $1224$ and $7320$ are not.)

(a) Compute the sum of all monotone numbers with five digits.

(b) Determine the number of final zeros in the decimal representation of the least common multiple of all monotone numbers (with no restriction on the number of digits).

The incircle $\gamma$ of triangle $ABC$ touches the side $AB$ at $T$. Let $D$ be the point of $\gamma$ diametrically opposite to $T$, and let $S$ be the intersection of the line $CD$ with the side $AB$. Prove that $AT = SB$.

A square is filled with $100$ lamps arranged in $10$ rows and $10$ columns. Some of them are on and the others are off. Each lamp has a push-button which, when pressed, switches the state of all lamps in its row and its column (including the lamp itself).

(a) Determine the initial states from which it is possible to switch on all the lamps.

(b) What is the answer if the square has $81$ lamps in $9$ rows and $9$ columns?
Find all three-digit positive integers that are equal to $34$ times the sum of their digits.

The ground plan of a house has the shape of an L, obtained by placing four squares of side $10$ metres side by side in a suitable way. The side walls are all $10$ metres high, and the roof of the house has six faces, starting from the six side walls and inclined at $30^\circ$ to a horizontal plane. Determine the volume of the house (that is, of the solid bounded by the six faces of the roof, the six side walls and the horizontal plane).

Let $r$ be a line in the plane and let $A$, $B$ be two points not on $r$. Let $R$ and $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and $B$ to $r$ respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $ARM$ and $BSM$ are equal (assuming the triangles are not degenerate).
Determine for which values of $n$ all the solutions of the equation $X^3 - 3X + n = 0$ are integers.
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $m = 5^n + 3^n + 1$. Prove that if $m$ is prime, then $n$ is a multiple of $12$.

A board with $100$ rows and $100$ columns has all its cells white.

(a) Is it possible to colour an odd number of cells so that every coloured cell has an odd number of adjacent coloured cells?

(b) Is it possible to colour some cells so that an odd number of them have exactly $4$ adjacent coloured cells and all the other coloured cells have exactly $2$ adjacent coloured cells?

(c) Is it possible to colour some cells so that an odd number of them have exactly $2$ adjacent coloured cells and all the other coloured cells have exactly $4$ adjacent coloured cells?

(Two cells are adjacent if they share a side.)
Find all three-digit positive integers $n$ $(100 \le n \le 999)$ that are equal to the number formed by the last three digits of $n^2$.

A museum has a square plan and is divided into $n^2$ equal square rooms $(n > 1)$. Every pair of adjacent rooms (i.e. rooms sharing a wall) is connected by a door (as in the example in the figure for $n = 4$). The night watchman wants to organise his inspection round according to the following rules: he starts in some room, where he stays for one minute; then he moves to an adjacent room, where he stays for another minute; the round continues through adjacent rooms, and in each room he always stays exactly one minute before moving on. He may pass through the same room several times, but at the end of the round (which does not necessarily end in the starting room) he must have spent exactly $k$ minutes in each of the $n^2$ rooms. Determine for which positive integers $n$ and $k$ such a round can be organised.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2003_p2_fig.png

In the figure, the point $C$ lies on the radius $OB$ of a semicircle with center $O$, and the segment $CD$ is perpendicular to the diameter $AB$. A circle with center $P$ is inscribed as shown: it is tangent to the arc $BD$ at $F$, to the segment $CD$ at $E$ and to the diameter $AB$ at $G$. Prove that triangle $ADG$ is isosceles.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2003_p3_fig.png

On an island there are two kinds of people: knights, who always tell the truth, and knaves, who always lie. One day the grand council, consisting of $2003$ members, meets. They sit at random around a round table, and during the meeting each of them declares: "Both my neighbours are knaves." The next day the council meets again, but one of its members is ill, so only $2002$ members are present. They again sit at random around the round table, and each of them says: "Both my neighbours belong to the category opposite to mine." Was the ill member a knave or a knight?

Given an $m \times n$ grid $(m, n \ge 1)$, a token is placed at the center of every cell and at every vertex of the grid (in the example in the figure, with $n = 4$ and $m = 3$, $32$ tokens are placed).

(a) Find all grids with exactly $500$ tokens.

(b) Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $k$ for which no grid has exactly $k$ tokens.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2003_p5_fig.png

$n$ people have been invited to a dinner and will sit around a round table whose seats have been marked with place cards numbered $1$ to $n$, arranged by a master of ceremonies. The waiter has decided to serve the courses in an original way: he chooses a guest and serves them, then moves counterclockwise by a number of seats equal to the number on the place card of the guest just served, serves the guest in that seat, and so on, always moving counterclockwise by the place-card number of the last guest served. Determine for which $n$ the master of ceremonies can arrange the place cards so that the waiter, starting from a suitable guest and following this procedure, serves all the guests.

Looking at the temperatures recorded in Cesenatico last December and January, Stefano noticed a strange coincidence: on every day of this period (except the first and the last), the minimum temperature was the sum of the minimum temperatures of the previous day and of the following day. Knowing that the minimum temperature was $5$ degrees on December $3$ and $2$ degrees on January $31$, determine the minimum temperature on December $25$.

Given two parallel lines $r$, $s$ in the plane and two points $P \in r$, $Q \in s$, consider pairs of circles $(C_P, C_Q)$ such that $C_P$ is tangent to $r$ at $P$, $C_Q$ is tangent to $s$ at $Q$, and the two circles are externally tangent to each other at a point $T$. Find the locus of the points $T$ as the pair of circles varies over all possibilities.

(a) Determine whether $2005^{2004}$ is a sum of two positive perfect squares.

(b) Determine whether $2004^{2005}$ is a sum of two positive perfect squares.

Let $P$ be a point inside a triangle $ABC$. The lines $AP$, $BP$, $CP$ meet the sides of $ABC$ at $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ respectively. Setting
$$x = \frac{AP}{PA'}, \qquad y = \frac{BP}{PB'}, \qquad z = \frac{CP}{PC'},$$
prove that $xyz = x + y + z + 2$.

Let $ABC$ be a right triangle with hypotenuse $AC$, and let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $B$ to $AC$. Knowing that the lengths $AB$, $BC$ and $BH$ are the sides of a new right triangle, determine the possible values of $\dfrac{AH}{CH}$.
Prove that among any $18$ consecutive positive integers not exceeding $2005$ there is at least one that is divisible by the sum of its digits.

Each cell of a $4 \times 4$ table contains the digit $1$ or the digit $2$. The sum of the $9$ digits in each of the four $3 \times 3$ squares contained in the table is a multiple of $4$, while the sum of all $16$ digits is not a multiple of $4$. Determine the largest and the smallest possible value of the sum of all $16$ digits.

Determine for which $n \ge 3$ it is possible to find $n$ positive integers such that any two of them have a common factor greater than $1$, but any three of them are relatively prime. If one adds the condition that all the numbers are less than $5000$, what is the largest possible value of $n$?

Let $h$ be a positive integer and let $(a_n)$ be the sequence defined by $a_0 = 1$ and
$$a_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a_n}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is even}, \\[4pt] a_n + h & \text{if } a_n \text{ is odd}. \end{cases}$$
(For example, if $h = 27$, then $a_1 = 28$, $a_2 = 14$, $a_3 = 7$, $a_4 = 34$, $a_5 = 17$, $a_6 = 44$, $\dots$) For which values of $h$ is there an $n > 0$ with $a_n = 1$?

Two circles $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ in the plane, with centers $A$ and $B$ respectively, meet at two points $C$ and $D$. Suppose that the circle through $A$, $B$, $C$ meets $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ again at $E$ and $F$ respectively, and that the arc $EF$ not containing $C$ lies outside the two discs bounded by $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$. Prove that the arc $EF$ not containing $C$ is bisected by the line $CD$.

Rosa and Savino play the following game with Neapolitan cards ($40$ cards numbered from $1$ to $10$ in $4$ different suits). Initially they share the $40$ cards ($20$ each); then, in turn, each of them places a card on the table. When some of the cards on the table have values adding up to exactly $15$, these cards are removed from the game (if there are several ways to obtain $15$, the player who placed the last card decides which cards with total $15$ to remove). At the end of the game, $2$ cards remain in Savino's hand (a $5$ and a $3$), one card on the table (a $9$) and one card in Rosa's hand. What is the value of Rosa's card?
Find all values of $m$, $n$, $p$ such that $p^n + 144 = m^2$, where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers and $p$ is a prime.

Let $\Gamma$ be a circle and let $A$, $B$ be two distinct points of $\Gamma$ that are not diametrically opposite. Let $P$ be a variable point of $\Gamma$ different from $A$ and $B$, and let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABP$. Determine the locus described by $H$ as $P$ varies.

On an infinite board, the positive integers are written in order along a spiral: one starts from $1$ and proceeds outwards, turning counterclockwise, as in the figure. A right ray of the board is the set of cells consisting of a cell $C$ and all cells in the row of $C$ to the right of $C$.

(a) Prove that there is a right ray whose cells contain no multiple of $3$.

(b) Determine whether there are infinitely many pairwise disjoint right rays whose cells contain no multiple of $3$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2006_p4_fig.png

Consider the inequality
$$(x_1 + \cdots + x_n)^2 \ge 4(x_1x_2 + x_2x_3 + \cdots + x_nx_1).$$

(a) Determine for which $n \ge 3$ it holds for every choice of positive real numbers $x_1, \dots, x_n$.

(b) Determine for which $n \ge 3$ it holds for every choice of real numbers $x_1, \dots, x_n$.

Alberto and Barbara play the following game. Initially there are some piles of tokens on a table (the number of tokens may vary from pile to pile). In turn, starting with Alberto, each player makes exactly one of the following moves:

• remove one token from a pile of their choice and eliminate it from the game;

• split a pile into two smaller piles, each with at least one token (without adding or removing tokens from the table).

The player who removes the last token from the table wins. Determine, according to the number of piles on the table at the start and how many tokens they contain, which of the two players has a winning strategy.

A regular hexagon is given in the plane. For every point $P$ of the plane, let $l(P)$ be the sum of the six distances from $P$ to the lines containing the sides of the hexagon, and let $v(P)$ be the sum of the six distances from $P$ to the vertices of the hexagon.

(a) For which points $P$ of the plane is $l(P)$ minimal?

(b) For which points $P$ of the plane is $v(P)$ minimal?

Two polynomials $p$ and $q$ with integer coefficients are called similar if they have the same degree and the same coefficients up to order.

(a) Prove that if $p$ and $q$ are similar, then $p(2007) - q(2007)$ is a multiple of $2$.

(b) Are there integers $k > 2$ such that for any two similar polynomials $p$ and $q$, $p(2007) - q(2007)$ is a multiple of $k$?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with centroid $G$. Let $D \ne A$ be a point on the line $AG$ such that $AG = GD$, and let $E \ne B$ be a point on the line $GB$ such that $GB = GE$. Finally, let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Prove that the quadrilateral $BMCD$ is cyclic if and only if $BA = BE$.

To celebrate Barbara's birthday, Alberto proposes the following game. Starting from the set of numbers $0, 1, \dots, 1024$, Barbara removes $2^9$ numbers from the set. Next, Alberto removes $2^8$ of the remaining numbers. Then Barbara removes $2^7$ of the remaining numbers, and so on, until only $2$ numbers $a$ and $b$ remain. At this point Alberto must pay Barbara $|a - b|$ euros. Determine the largest amount of euros that Barbara can be sure to collect, whatever strategy Alberto adopts.
The sequence $(x_n)$ is defined by $x_1 = 2$ and $x_{n+1} = 2x_n^2 - 1$ for $n \ge 1$. Prove that $n$ and $x_n$ are relatively prime for every $n \ge 1$.

For every integer $n \ge 2$, determine:

(a) the largest real number $c_n$ such that
$$\frac{1}{1+a_1} + \frac{1}{1+a_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{1+a_n} \ge c_n$$
for all positive reals $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ with $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = 1$;

(b) the largest real number $d_n$ such that
$$\frac{1}{1+2a_1} + \frac{1}{1+2a_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{1+2a_n} \ge d_n$$
for all positive reals $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ with $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = 1$.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. All cells of an $n \times n$ board are coloured red or blue so that every $2 \times 2$ square contained in the board has exactly two red cells and two blue cells. How many such colourings are there? (Two colourings obtained from each other by a rotation or a reflection of the board are considered distinct.)

Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers such that
$$a^2 + 2^{b+1} = 3^c.$$

Francesca and Giorgia play the following game. Initially there are some columns of coins on a table; each column contains some number of coins, which may vary from column to column. In turn, each player makes exactly one of the following moves:

• choose a column containing a nonzero even number $2k$ of coins and replace it by two columns of $k$ coins each;

• remove from the table all columns containing an odd number of coins.

If a move of the first kind is not possible, the player must make a move of the second kind, and vice versa. Francesca starts. The player who removes the last coin from the table wins.

(a) If initially there is a single column on the table, containing $2008^{2008}$ coins, which player has a winning strategy?

(b) For which initial configurations does Francesca have a winning strategy?

Let $a < b < c < d < e$ be real numbers. All $10$ possible sums of two of these $5$ numbers are computed. The three smallest of these sums are $32$, $36$, $37$, and the two largest are $48$ and $51$. Determine all possible values of $e$.

Let $ABCD$ be a square with center $O$. Two congruent isosceles triangles $BCJ$ and $CDK$ are constructed outside the square, with bases $BC$ and $CD$ respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $CJ$. Prove that the lines $OM$ and $BK$ are perpendicular.

A flea starts at the point $(0, 0)$ of the Cartesian plane and then makes $n$ jumps. Each jump is made in one of the four cardinal directions, as the flea chooses. The first jump has length $1$, the second length $2$, the third length $4$, and so on, up to the $n$-th jump, which has length $2^{n-1}$. Prove that if the final position of the flea is known, then its position after each of the $n$ jumps can be determined uniquely.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene acute triangle, $\Gamma$ its circumcircle, and $K$ the foot of the bisector from vertex $A$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ containing $A$. Let $A'$ be the second intersection of $MK$ with $\Gamma$, and let $T$ be the intersection of the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $A'$. Let $R$ be the intersection of the perpendicular to $AK$ through $A$ and the perpendicular to $A'K$ through $A'$. Prove that $T$, $R$ and $K$ are collinear.

A positive integer $k$ is called $n$-squared if, however the cells of a $2n \times k$ board are coloured with $n$ different colours, there exist $4$ distinct cells of the same colour whose centers are the vertices of a rectangle with sides parallel to the sides of the board. Determine, in terms of $n$, the smallest positive integer $k$ that is $n$-squared.

$N < 40$ people take a mathematics test, and the pass mark is $65$. The results are as follows: the average of all participants is $66$, that of those who passed is $71$, and that of those who failed is $56$. However, because of a mistake in the wording of a question, all scores are increased by $5$. At this point the average of those who passed becomes $75$ and that of those who failed becomes $59$.

(a) Find all possible values of $N$.

(b) Find all possible values of $N$ in the case where, after the increase, the average of those who passed became $79$ and that of those who failed $47$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $\angle CAB = \angle CDA$ and $\angle BCA = \angle ACD$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Prove that $\angle BCM = \angle DBA$.

In the trapezoid $ABCD$ the sides $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel, and the angles $\angle ABC$ and $\angle BAD$ are acute. Prove that it is possible to divide triangle $ABC$ into $4$ disjoint triangles $X_1, \dots, X_4$ and triangle $ABD$ into $4$ disjoint triangles $Y_1, \dots, Y_4$ so that the triangles $X_i$ and $Y_i$ are congruent for every $i$.

Prove that there are infinitely many primes that divide at least one integer of the form
$$2^{n^3+1} - 3^{n^2+1} + 5^{n+1}$$
with $n$ a positive integer.

A trapezoid has bases of lengths $1$ and $4$. It is divided into two trapezoids by a cut parallel to the bases, of length $3$. We now want to divide the two new trapezoids, again by cuts parallel to the bases, into $m$ and $n$ trapezoids respectively, so that all $m + n$ trapezoids obtained have the same area. Determine the smallest possible value of $m + n$ and the lengths of the cuts that achieve it.

A sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ is called a ladder of length $n$ if it consists of $n$ consecutive numbers in increasing order.

(a) Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there are two ladders of length $n$ with no common elements, $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$, such that $\gcd(a_i, b_i) = 1$ for every $i$ from $1$ to $n$.

(b) Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there are two ladders of length $n$ with no common elements, $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$, such that $\gcd(a_i, b_i) > 1$ for every $i$ from $1$ to $n$.

Some integers between $1$ and $7$ are written on a blackboard. Not all the numbers from $1$ to $7$ need to be present, and some or all of them may be repeated, one or more times. A move consists of choosing one or more of the numbers on the board, all different, erasing them, and writing in their place the numbers that together with the erased ones form the whole set $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$. For example, the following moves are allowed:

• erase a $4$ and a $5$, and write the numbers $1$, $2$, $3$, $6$, $7$ in their place;

• erase a $1$, a $2$, a $3$, a $4$, a $5$, a $6$ and a $7$ without writing anything.

Prove that if some sequence of moves, starting from the initial situation, leaves a single number on the board (written once), then this number does not depend on the sequence of moves used.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, and let $P$ be the intersection of the external bisectors of $\angle DAC$ and $\angle DBC$. Prove that $\angle APD = \angle BPC$ if and only if $AD + AC = BC + BD$. (The external bisector of an angle is the line through its vertex perpendicular to the internal bisector.)

Find all solutions $(p, n)$ of the equation
$$n^3 = p^2 - p - 1,$$
where $p$ is a prime and $n$ is an integer.

On the sides of a triangle $ABC$ with a right angle at $A$, three points $D$, $E$, $F$ are chosen (on $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ respectively) so that the quadrilateral $AFDE$ is a square. If $x$ is the length of its side, prove that
$$\frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{AB} + \frac{1}{AC}.$$
Find all positive integers that are equal to $300$ times the sum of their digits.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. There are $n$ people standing in a line, each of whom is either a knave (who always lies) or a knight (who always tells the truth). Every person except the first points at one of the people in front of them and declares either "This person is a knave" or "This person is a knight". Knowing that there are strictly more knaves than knights, prove that by listening to the statements one can determine, for every person, whether they are a knave or a knight.

Let $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ be the sequence defined by
$$x_1 = 4, \qquad x_{n+1} = x_1 x_2 x_3 \cdots x_n + 5 \quad \text{for } n \ge 1.$$
(So the first terms are $x_1 = 4$, $x_2 = 4 + 5 = 9$, $x_3 = 4 \cdot 9 + 5 = 41$, $\dots$) Find all pairs $\{a, b\}$ of positive integers such that $x_a x_b$ is a perfect square.

Let $ABCD$ be a square. Describe the locus of points $P$ of the plane, different from $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, such that
$$\angle APB + \angle CPD = 180^\circ.$$

Find all pairs $\{a, b\}$ of positive integers with the following property: however the positive integers are coloured with two colours $A$ and $B$, there are always two positive integers of colour $A$ whose difference is $a$, or two positive integers of colour $B$ whose difference is $b$.

In triangle $ABC$, suppose that $a > b$, where $a = BC$ and $b = AC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the incircles of triangles $ACM$ and $BCM$ respectively. Let $A'$ and $B'$ be the points where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ touch $CM$. Prove that
$$A'B' = \frac{a - b}{2}.$$

Every integer is coloured with one of two colours, red or blue. For every finite set $A$ of consecutive integers, the absolute value of the difference between the number of red integers and the number of blue integers in $A$ is at most $1000$. Prove that there is a set of $2000$ consecutive integers containing exactly $1000$ red numbers and $1000$ blue numbers.
In which bases $b > 6$ does the representation $5654$ denote a power of a prime?

Two magicians perform the following trick. First, the first magician shuts the second one in a booth where he can neither see nor hear anything. To begin, the first magician invites Daniele, a member of the audience, to place on each cell of an $n \times n$ board, as he likes, a white or a black token. Then he asks Daniele to point out a cell $C$ of his choice. At this point the first magician chooses a cell $D$ (not necessarily different from $C$) and replaces the token on $D$ with one of the other colour (white with black or black with white). The booth is then opened. Looking at the board, the second magician manages to guess the cell $C$. For which $n$ can the two magicians agree on a strategy so that the trick always succeeds?

For every three-digit positive integer $n$ (so with first digit different from zero), let $n'$ be the number obtained from $n$ by deleting its digits equal to zero, if any. For example, if $n = 205$ then $n' = 25$. Determine the number of three-digit integers $n$ for which $n'$ is a divisor of $n$ different from $n$.

For every positive integer $n$, let $D_n$ be the greatest common divisor of all numbers of the form $a^n + (a+1)^n + (a+2)^n$, as $a$ ranges over all positive integers.

(a) Prove that for every $n$, $D_n$ is of the form $3^k$ for some integer $k \ge 0$.

(b) Prove that for every $k \ge 0$ there is an integer $n$ with $D_n = 3^k$.

On a circle with center $A$ and radius $R$, four distinct points $B$, $C$, $G$, $H$ are taken in this order so that $G$ lies on the extension of the median of triangle $ABC$ from $B$, and $H$ lies on the extension of the altitude of $ABC$ from $B$. If $X$ is the intersection of the lines $AC$ and $GH$, prove that the segment $AX$ has length $2R$.
Prove that there is a positive integer that can be written as a sum of $2015$ distinct $2014$-th powers of positive integers $x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{2015}$ in at least two ways.

A $(2n+1) \times (2n+1)$ board, with $n > 0$, is coloured so that every cell is white or black. A cell is called special if there are at least $n$ other cells of the same colour in its row and at least $n$ other cells of the same colour in its column.

(a) Prove that there are at least $2n + 1$ special cells.

(b) Give an example with at most $4n$ special cells.

(c) Determine, in terms of $n$, the smallest possible number of special cells.

A rectangular box $ABCDA'B'C'D'$ is given, where $ABCD$ is the bottom face with the letters assigned clockwise, and $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie below $A'$, $B'$, $C'$, $D'$ respectively. The box is divided into eight pieces by three mutually perpendicular planes parallel to its faces. For every vertex $P$ of the box, let $V_P$ be the volume of the piece containing $P$. Knowing that $V_A = 40$, $V_C = 300$, $V_{B'} = 360$ and $V_{C'} = 90$, what is the volume of the box $ABCDA'B'C'D'$?

A music streaming service offers songs classified into $10$ genres, each song belonging to exactly one genre. The songs are played one after another: the first $17$ are chosen by the user, but from the eighteenth on the service decides automatically which song to play. Elisabetta has noticed that if one ranks the genres according to how many times they occur among the last $17$ songs played, the new song always belongs to the genre at the top of the ranking or, in case of a tie, to one of the genres tied for first place. Prove that, however the first $17$ songs are chosen, from some point on all the songs played belong to the same genre.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, let $K$ be the foot of the angle bisector from $A$ to $BC$, and let $J$ be the foot of the angle trisector from $A$ to $BC$ closer to the side $AC$ (i.e. $J$ is the point on $BC$ such that $3\angle CAJ = \angle CAB$). Let $C'$ and $B'$ be points on the line $AJ$, on the same side of $A$ as $J$, such that $AC' = AC$ and $AB' = AB$. Prove that the quadrilateral $ABB'C$ is cyclic if and only if the lines $C'K$ and $B'B$ are parallel.

Find all pairs of integers $(a, b)$ satisfying
$$a^3 + b^3 + 3ab = 1.$$

Let $\Gamma$ be a circle, $AB$ a chord of it, $C$ a point inside the segment $AB$, and $r$ a line through $C$ meeting $\Gamma$ at $D$ and $E$, which lie on opposite sides of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Let $\Gamma_D$ be the circle externally tangent to $\Gamma$ at $D$ and tangent to $AB$ at a point $F$, and let $\Gamma_E$ be the circle externally tangent to $\Gamma$ at $E$ and tangent to $AB$ at a point $G$. Prove that $CA = CB$ if and only if $CF = CG$.

Ada and Charles play a game. Initially an integer $n > 1$ is written on the blackboard. In turn, Ada and Charles erase the number $k$ on the board and replace it

1. either by a positive divisor of $k$ different from $1$ and from $k$ itself,

2. or by $k + 1$.

Initially each player has one thousand points. When a player makes move 1 they gain a point; when they make move 2 they lose a point. The game ends when one of the players reaches zero points, and this player loses. Ada moves first. For which values of $n$ does Charles have a winning strategy?
Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ and $E$ be the projections of $A$ onto the angle bisectors from $B$ and $C$. Prove that $DE$ is parallel to $BC$.

In a mathematics competition $3$ problems are set, each scored with an integer from $0$ to $7$ (inclusive). It is known that for any two contestants there is at most one problem on which they obtained the same score (for example, there are no two contestants whose scores on the three problems are $7, 1, 2$ for the first and $7, 5, 2$ for the second, but there could be two contestants with scores $7, 1, 2$ and $7, 2, 1$). What is the largest possible number of contestants?

Let $\Gamma$ be the excircle of triangle $ABC$ opposite to vertex $A$, i.e. the circle tangent to $BC$ and to the extensions of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ beyond $B$ and $C$. Let $D$ be the center of $\Gamma$, and let $E$ and $F$ be the points where $\Gamma$ touches the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $J$ be the intersection of the segments $BD$ and $EF$. Prove that the angle $\angle CJB$ is a right angle.
Find all pairs of positive integers $(a, n)$ with $a \ge n \ge 2$ for which the number $(a+1)^n + a - 1$ is a power of $2$.

Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ be the sequence of rational numbers defined as follows: $x_0$ is an arbitrary rational number and, for $n \ge 0$,
$$x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \left| \dfrac{x_n}{2} - 1 \right| & \text{if the numerator of } x_n \text{ is even}, \\[6pt] \left| \dfrac{1}{x_n} - 1 \right| & \text{if the numerator of } x_n \text{ is odd}, \end{cases}$$
where the numerator of a rational number means that of the fraction in lowest terms. Prove that for every value of $x_0$:

(a) the sequence contains only finitely many distinct terms;

(b) the sequence contains exactly one of the numbers $0$ and $2/3$ (i.e. either there is an index $k$ with $x_k = 0$, or there is an index $m$ with $x_m = 2/3$, but not both).

A mysterious machine contains a secret combination consisting of $2016$ integers $x_1, \dots, x_{2016}$. It is known that all numbers of the combination are equal except one. One can query the machine by submitting a sequence of $2016$ integers $y_1, \dots, y_{2016}$; the machine answers by revealing the value of the sum $x_1y_1 + \cdots + x_{2016}y_{2016}$. After answering the first question, the machine accepts a second one, then a third, and so on. How many questions are needed to determine the combination:

(a) knowing that the different number is equal to zero?

(b) not knowing what the different number is?

Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Consider a regular hexagon of side $a$, and construct on its sides six rectangles with sides $a$ and $b$, lying outside the hexagon. The twelve new vertices lie on a circle. Repeat the operation with the values of $a$ and $b$ exchanged: start from a regular hexagon of side $b$ and construct on it, again outside the hexagon, six rectangles with sides $a$ and $b$. The twelve new vertices lie on a second circle. Prove that the two circles have the same radius.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Consider the solutions $(a, b, c)$ of the system
$$\begin{cases} n = a + b - c \\ n = a^2 + b^2 - c^2 \end{cases}$$
where $a$, $b$, $c$ are integers. Prove that there is at least one solution and that there are finitely many solutions.

The witch Magò has a deck of $52$ cards, stacked face down. Magò takes the packet formed by the seven cards on top of the pile, turns it over and puts it at the bottom of the pile. Now all the cards are again in a pile, but not all of them are face down: the seven at the bottom are face up. Magò repeats this operation until, for the first time again, all the cards are face down. In total, how many packets of seven cards has Magò turned over?

$ABCD$ is a tetrahedron with the following property: if $A'$, $B'$, $C'$, $D'$ are the incenters of the faces $BCD$, $ACD$, $ABD$ and $ABC$ respectively, then the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ and $DD'$ have a common point. Prove that the product of the lengths of two opposite edges of the tetrahedron is constant, i.e.
$$AB \cdot CD = AC \cdot BD = AD \cdot BC.$$
Let $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that $x_{mn} \ne x_{m(n+1)}$ for all positive integers $m$, $n$. Prove that there is a positive integer $i$ with $x_i \ge 2017$.

Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $m$ such that the number of distinct odd prime factors of $m(m+3)$ is a multiple of $3$. (For example, $60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ has two distinct odd prime factors and $1050 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7$ has three.)

A cone-shaped bottle stands on its base. It is filled with water until the level of the liquid is $8$ centimetres below the vertex of the cone, measured vertically. If the bottle is now turned upside down, without changing the amount of water inside, the empty space left at the top of the inverted cone is $2$ centimetres high. How tall is the bottle?

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB \ne AC$ and centroid $G$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, let $\Gamma$ be the circle with center $G$ and radius $GM$, and let $N$ be the intersection of $\Gamma$ with $BC$ other than $M$. Let $S$ be the reflection of $A$ in $N$, i.e. the point on the line $AN$ such that $AN = NS$ $(A \ne S)$. Prove that $GS$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive integers. Suppose that, in their decimal representations, none of the $x_i$ is an extension of another $x_j$. (For example, $123$ is an extension of $12$ and $459$ is an extension of $4$, but $134$ is not an extension of $123$.) Prove that
$$\frac{1}{x_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{x_n} < 3.$$

Let $N > 1$ be an integer. Let $x$ be the smallest positive integer with the following property: there is a positive integer $y$ strictly less than $x - 1$ such that $x$ divides $N + y$. Prove that $x$ is either twice a prime or a power of a prime. (Recall that $x$ is a power of a prime if $x = p^n$ for some prime $p$ and integer $n \ge 1$.)

Given a real number $x$ between $0$ and $1$, consider its decimal representation $0.c_1c_2c_3\dots$ Let $B(x)$ be the set of distinct blocks of six consecutive digits that occur in the sequence $c_1c_2c_3\dots$ For example, $B(1/22) = \{045454, 454545, 545454\}$. Determine the minimum number of elements of $B(x)$ as $x$ ranges over the irrational numbers between $0$ and $1$ (i.e. those whose decimal expansion is neither finite nor eventually periodic).

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$ and incenter $I$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. The lines $BI$ and $CI$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $M$ and $N$ respectively. Let $D$ be another point of $\Gamma$ on the arc $BC$ not containing $A$, and let $E$, $F$ be the intersections of $AD$ with $BI$ and with $CI$ respectively. Finally, let $P$ and $Q$ be the intersections of $DM$ with $CI$ and of $DN$ with $BI$ respectively.

(i) Prove that the points $D$, $I$, $P$, $Q$ lie on a circle $\Omega$.

(ii) Prove that the lines $CE$ and $BF$ meet on $\Omega$.
Let $ABCDEF$ be a hexagon inscribed in a circle such that $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$ and $EF = FA$. Prove that the segments $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ are concurrent.
Let $p$, $q$ be primes. Prove that if $p + q^2$ is a perfect square, then $p^2 + q^n$ is not a perfect square for any positive integer $n$.

Let $n > 2$ be an integer. We want to colour red exactly $n + 1$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 2n-1, 2n$ so that there are no three distinct red numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ with $x + y = z$. Prove that there is one and only one way of choosing the numbers to colour red satisfying this condition.

Let $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denote the largest integer $\le x$. Let $\lambda \ge 1$ be a real number and $n$ a positive integer such that $\lfloor \lambda^{n+1} \rfloor, \lfloor \lambda^{n+2} \rfloor, \dots, \lfloor \lambda^{4n} \rfloor$ are all perfect squares. Prove that $\lfloor \lambda \rfloor$ is a perfect square.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Let $D$ be the foot of the internal bisector from $A$, and $M$ the midpoint of $AD$. Let $X$ be a point on the segment $BM$ such that $\angle MXA = \angle DAC$. Prove that $AX$ is perpendicular to $XC$.

Alberto and Barbara sit side by side at a table on which they have placed $15$ chocolates in a row, from left to right. Some of the chocolates are milk chocolates and the others dark chocolates. In turn, starting with Alberto, they play the following game: on their turn, each player must eat a positive number of consecutive chocolates, always starting from the leftmost of the remaining ones, in such a way that the number of eaten chocolates of the same type as the first one is odd. (For example, if at some turn the remaining sequence is $LLFLF$, where $L$ stands for milk and $F$ for dark, the player may eat the first chocolate from the left, the first $4$ from the left, or all $5$ chocolates.) The player who eats the last chocolate wins. Among the $2^{15}$ possible initial sequences of flavours, for how many does Barbara have a winning strategy?

Five points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ lie on a circle in this order. Suppose that the lines $BC$ and $DE$ meet at a point $F$, that $F$ and $A$ lie on opposite sides of the line $BE$, and that the circumcircle of triangle $BFE$ is tangent (at $E$) to the line $AE$.

(a) Prove that the lines $AC$ and $DE$ are parallel.

(b) Prove that $AE = CD$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2020}$ and $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{2020}$ be real numbers, not necessarily distinct. Suppose that there are only finitely many positive integers $n$ for which the equation
$$a_1|x - b_1| + a_2|x - b_2| + \cdots + a_{2020}|x - b_{2020}| = n \qquad (1)$$
has exactly two real solutions. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers $n$ for which equation (1) has at least one real solution.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$, and let $E$ be the second intersection of the side $BC$ with the circumcircle of triangle $CDM$. Prove that the lines $AE$, $BM$ and $CD$ pass through a common point if and only if $CE = CM$.

Each cell of an $8 \times 8$ table is inhabited by a knight or a knave. As tradition has it, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. All the inhabitants of the table state: "The number of knaves in my column is (strictly) greater than the number of knaves in my row." Determine how many configurations are compatible with this statement.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$. Let $D$ be the reflection of $I$ in the side $AB$, and $E$ the reflection of $I$ in the side $AC$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $BID$ and $CIE$ are tangent to each other.

A grid consists of $n \times n$ points, $n$ a positive integer. Sentinels are placed at some of these points. Each sentinel chooses two mutually perpendicular directions (among the directions of the rows and columns of the grid) and watches all the points lying in the chosen directions. Each sentinel also watches the point it occupies, and sentinels on the border may end up looking into the void, depending on the directions chosen. For example, in the figure, showing $5$ sentinels in a $4 \times 4$ grid, the sentinels at $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ watch $1$, $3$, $4$, $5$, $7$ points respectively; the points $D$ and $E$ are watched by a single sentinel, the point $C$ by $2$ sentinels, and the points $A$, $B$ and $F$ by $3$ sentinels.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2021_p3_fig.png

(a) Prove that $12$ sentinels can be placed in a $4 \times 4$ grid so that every point of the grid is watched by at most $2$ sentinels.

(b) Let $S(n)$ be the largest number of sentinels that can be placed in an $n \times n$ grid so that every point of the grid is watched by at most $2$ sentinels. Prove that $3n \le S(n) \le 4n$ for every $n \ge 3$.

Given two fractions $a/b$ and $c/d$, define their pirate sum as
$$\frac{a}{b} \diamond \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a+c}{b+d},$$
where the two initial fractions are in lowest terms, and the result is then reduced to lowest terms as well. For example, the pirate sum of $2/7$ and $4/5$ is $1/2$. Given an integer $n \ge 3$, the fractions
$$\frac{1}{1},\ \frac{1}{2},\ \frac{1}{3},\ \dots,\ \frac{1}{n}$$
are initially written on the blackboard. At each move we choose two fractions on the board, erase them and write their pirate sum in their place. We continue until only one fraction remains on the board. Determine, in terms of $n$, the largest and the smallest possible value of this last fraction.

A sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n, \dots$ consists of an initial block of $p$ distinct positive integers, which then repeat periodically. This means that $\{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p\}$ are $p$ distinct positive integers and $x_{n+p} = x_n$ for every positive integer $n$. The terms of the sequence are not known, and the goal is to find the period $p$. To do this, at each step one may reveal the value of a term of the sequence of one's choice (the choice may depend on the outcome of the previous steps).

(a) Knowing in advance that $1 \le p \le 10$, determine the smallest $n$ for which there is a strategy that finds $p$ with certainty by revealing at most $n$ terms.

(b) Knowing in advance that $p$ is one of the first $k$ primes, determine for which values of $k$ there is a strategy that finds $p$ with certainty by revealing at most $5$ terms.

$n = 10\,000$ contestants take part in a mathematics competition. At the closing party, one after another, the first contestant takes $1/n$ of the cake, the second takes $2/n$ of the remaining cake, the third takes $3/n$ of the cake left after the first two have helped themselves, and so on until the last one, who takes all the remaining cake. Determine which contestant takes the largest piece of cake.

Alberto chooses $2022$ integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2022}$ (not necessarily positive and not necessarily distinct) and arranges them in a $2022 \times 2022$ table so that the cell $(i, j)$ contains the number $a_k$ with $k = \max(i, j)$:
$$\begin{array}{cccccc} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 & a_4 & \cdots & a_n \\ a_2 & a_2 & a_3 & a_4 & \cdots & a_n \\ a_3 & a_3 & a_3 & a_4 & \cdots & a_n \\ a_4 & a_4 & a_4 & a_4 & \cdots & a_n \\ \vdots & & & & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_n & a_n & a_n & a_n & \cdots & a_n \end{array}$$
(here $a_n$ stands for $a_{2022}$). Barbara does not know the numbers chosen by Alberto, but she knows how they were arranged in the table. Having fixed an integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le 2022$, Barbara wants to determine the value of $a_k$, and does not care about the values of the other $a_i$ with $i \ne k$. To do so, Barbara may ask Alberto one or more questions, in each of which she asks for the sum of the numbers in the cells of a path, where a path is an ordered list of cells such that:

• the path starts at the top-left cell and ends at the bottom-right cell;

• the cells of the path are all distinct;

• two consecutive cells of the path always share a side.

Determine, as $k$ varies, the minimum number of questions Barbara needs in order to determine $a_k$.

The robot Mag-o-matic handles $101$ glasses, arranged in a row whose positions are numbered from $1$ to $101$. Each glass may or may not contain a ball. Mag-o-matic only accepts elementary instructions of the form $(a; b, c)$, which it interprets as: "look at the glass in position $a$: if it contains a ball, swap the glasses in positions $b$ and $c$ (together with their contents, if any); otherwise, go on to the next instruction" (here $a$, $b$, $c$ are integers from $1$ to $101$, with $b \ne c$, but not necessarily different from $a$). A program is a finite sequence of elementary instructions, fixed in advance, which Mag-o-matic executes one after the other. A subset $S \subseteq \{0, 1, 2, \dots, 101\}$ is called identifiable if there is a program which, starting from any initial configuration, produces a final configuration in which the glass in position $1$ contains a ball if and only if the number of glasses containing a ball is an element of $S$.

(a) Prove that the subset of $\{0, 1, \dots, 101\}$ consisting of the odd numbers is identifiable.

(b) Determine all identifiable subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, 101\}$.

Let $ABC$ be a non-equilateral triangle and let $R$ be its circumradius. The incircle of $ABC$ has center $I$ and touches the side $CA$ at $D$ and the side $CB$ at $E$. Let $A_1$ be the point of the line $EI$ such that $A_1I = R$, with $I$ between $A_1$ and $E$, and let $B_1$ be the point of the line $DI$ such that $B_1I = R$, with $I$ between $B_1$ and $D$. Let $P$ be the intersection of the lines $AA_1$ and $BB_1$.

(a) Prove that $P$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

(b) Suppose moreover that $AB = 1$ and that $P$ coincides with $C$. Determine the possible values of the perimeter of $ABC$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that
$$54^a = a^b.$$
Prove that $a$ is a power of $54$, that is, there is a positive integer $c$ with $a = 54^c$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. On a blackboard, Bobo writes a list of $n$ non-negative integers. He then performs a sequence of moves, each of which is as follows:

• for each $i = 1, \dots, n$, he computes the number $a_i$ of integers currently on the board that are at most $i$;

• he erases all the integers on the board;

• he writes on the board the numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$.

For instance, if $n = 5$ and the numbers initially on the board are $0, 7, 2, 6, 2$, after the first move the numbers on the board are $1, 3, 3, 3, 3$, after the second they are $1, 1, 5, 5, 5$, and so on.

(a) Prove that, whatever $n$ and whatever the initial configuration, the numbers on the board eventually stop changing.

(b) Determine, in terms of $n$, the minimum integer $k$ such that, whatever the initial configuration, the moves from the $k$-th onwards no longer change the numbers on the board.

For a positive integer $n$, let $s(n)$ be the sum of the digits of $n$ (in its usual decimal representation). For example, $s(8) = 8$, $s(2023) = 7$, $s(573) = 15$.

(a) Determine whether there exist distinct positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $2023 \cdot a + s(a) = 2023 \cdot b + s(b)$.

(b) Determine whether there exist distinct positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a + 2023 \cdot s(a) = b + 2023 \cdot s(b)$.

Fix a point $C$ on a circle with center $O$ and diameter $AB$, with $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$. Now let $D$ vary among the points of the arc $AB$ not containing $C$ that are distinct from $A$ and $B$. Given $D$, let $E$ be the point of the segment $CD$ such that the lines $BE$ and $CD$ are perpendicular. Prove that the product $CE \cdot ED$ attains its maximum, as $D$ varies, precisely when $B$, $O$, $E$, $D$ lie on a circle.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers (positive, negative or zero) such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 6$.

(a) Determine the maximum possible value of the expression
$$(a - b)^2 + (b - c)^2 + (c - a)^2.$$

(b) Determine the maximum possible value of the expression
$$(a - b)^2 \cdot (b - c)^2 \cdot (c - a)^2.$$

In both cases, describe all the triples for which the maximum is attained.

Dedalo buys a finite number of binary strings, each of finite length and made up of the binary digits $0$ and $1$. For each string, he pays $(1/2)^L$ drachmas, where $L$ is the length of the string. The Minotaur is able to escape the labyrinth if he can find an infinite sequence of binary digits that does not contain any of the strings Dedalo bought. Dedalo's aim is to trap the Minotaur.

For instance, if Dedalo buys the strings $00$ and $11$ for a total of half a drachma, the Minotaur can escape using the infinite sequence $01010101\dots$ On the other hand, Dedalo can trap the Minotaur by spending $75$ cents of a drachma: he could for example buy the strings $0$ and $11$, or the strings $00$, $11$, $01$.

Determine all positive integers $c$ such that Dedalo can trap the Minotaur with an expense of at most $c$ cents of a drachma.

Jack writes on the blackboard the number $x_0 = 2024^{2024}$. Then he erases it and writes in its place $x_1 = |x_0 - \pi|$. Then he erases $x_1$ and writes in its place $x_2 = |x_1 - \pi|$, and so on. In other words, at each move Jack erases the previously written number $x_n$ and replaces it with $x_{n+1} = |x_n - \pi|$. Prove that there is a value of $n$ such that $x_{n+2} = x_n$.

A square of side $1$ is given in the plane. A point $M$ of the plane is called median if there are two points $P$ and $Q$ on the boundary of the square such that:

• the segment $PQ$ has length $1$;

• $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$.

Determine the set of all median points.

An integer $n$ is called Egyptian if there is a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers $0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k = n$ (so the last term of the sequence is $n$) such that
$$\frac{1}{a_1} + \frac{1}{a_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{a_k} = 1.$$

(a) Determine whether $n = 72$ is Egyptian.

(b) Determine whether $n = 71$ is Egyptian.

(c) Determine whether $n = 7271$ is Egyptian.

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle with $AB < BC$, inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$. Let $P$ be a point on the arc $BC$ (not containing $A$) and $Q$ a point on the arc $CD$ (not containing $A$) such that $BP = CQ$. The circle with diameter $AQ$ meets the line $AP$ again at $S$. The line through $B$ perpendicular to $AQ$ meets the line $AP$ at $X$.

(a) Prove that $XS = PS$.

(b) Prove that $AX = DQ$.

A fortress is a finite set of cells of an infinite square grid with the property that from every cell one can reach every other cell by always moving between cells sharing a side. The walls of the fortress are the unit segments of the grid separating a square of the fortress from a square not belonging to the fortress. The area $A$ of a fortress is the number of squares it consists of; the perimeter $P$ of a fortress is the total length of its walls. The figure shows three possible fortresses with their area and perimeter.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/italy_2024_p5_fig.png

Some cells of the fortress may contain a guard, who watches all the cells above, below, to the right or to the left of his position with no walls in between (each guard also watches the cell he stands in). For example, a guard placed in the cell with the dot in the first fortress watches six cells, including his own.

(a) Determine the smallest $k$ such that $k$ guards are enough to watch any fortress with perimeter $P \le 2024$.

(b) Determine the smallest $k$ such that $k$ guards are enough to watch any fortress with area $A \le 2024$.

For every positive integer $n$, determine the smallest real number $M_n$ such that
$$\frac{1}{a_1} + \frac{a_1}{a_2} + \frac{a_2}{a_3} + \cdots + \frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n} \le M_n$$
for every $n$-tuple $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ of integers with $1 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_n$.

For every positive integer $n$, let $s(n)$ be the sum of the digits of $n$ in its usual decimal representation. For example, $s(7) = 7$ and $s(10654) = 16$.

(a) Determine the smallest positive integer $n$ such that $n = 225 \cdot s(n)$.

(b) Determine the smallest positive integer $n$ such that $n = 225 \cdot s(n)^2$.

Determine for which integer values of $a$ the set of integers $x$ satisfying the inequality
$$10x^2 + a \le 33x$$
consists of exactly one element.

For a positive integer $n$, let $p(n)$ be the number of distinct primes dividing $n$. For example, $p(12) = 2$ and $p(120) = 3$. An integer $n$ is called balanced if $p(n)$ is even, and unbalanced if $p(n)$ is odd. Prove that there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive positive integers that are both balanced or both unbalanced.

A set $S$ is called aged if it consists of $2025$ distinct positive real numbers. For every aged set $S$, let $d(S)$ be the number of powers of $2$, with distinct positive integer exponents, that can be written as a sum of two distinct elements of $S$. Determine the maximum of $d(S)$ as $S$ ranges over all aged sets.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $D$ be the foot of the bisector from $A$. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $AD$ meets the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $E$ and $F$, with $E$ and $B$ on opposite sides of the line $AD$. Let $G$ be the intersection of $BE$ and $DF$, and let $H$ be the intersection of $CF$ and $DE$. Prove that the lines $GH$ and $BC$ are parallel.

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be two angles with positive measure less than $90^\circ$. An alphabet ant is a creature that advances in a straight line in the plane. The ant is extremely heavy, so it cannot be moved from one place to another; it can only be rotated, so that it stays at the same point but faces a different direction of the plane. We may choose the points where the rotations take place (as many as we like) and the new direction in which the ant is placed at each of them, but this is the only operation allowed. When it is rotated, the ant stops for an instant and may decide either to keep the new direction in which it has been placed, or to turn further by $\alpha$ clockwise, or by $\beta$ counterclockwise; then it resumes its march. If the ant passes again through a point where it has previously been rotated, it notices, gets scared, stops and does not move any more. Prove that for all admissible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ it is always possible to stop an alphabet ant with a finite number of rotations.

There are three types of coins, denominated in Altairian dollars (AD), worth $3$ AD, $5$ AD and $7$ AD. Andromeda would like to buy a snack from one of those wicked vending machines that do not give change. With the coins she has, she could buy a $29$ AD snack, but only by paying $32$ AD, and she has no way to do it with less. There is a $24$ AD snack: what is the least amount Andromeda has to spend to get it?

A hollow right cone of crispy wafer is $10$ cm high. A ball of ice cream is put into it, centred at a point $O$ on the axis of the cone and tangent to the lateral surface of the cone along the circumference of the base. Let $V$ be the vertex of the cone and $K$ the intersection point of the segment $VO$ with the surface of the sphere. Prove that the distance $VK$ between the vertex of the cone and the sphere is greater than $5$ cm.

(a) Determine all pairs of positive integers $n > m$ with the following property: there exists a positive integer $a$ such that the smallest prime dividing $n + a$ coincides with the smallest prime dividing $m + a$.

(b) Determine all pairs of positive integers $n > m$ with the following property: there exists a positive integer $a$ such that the smallest prime dividing $n + a$ coincides with the largest prime dividing $m + a$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$ not containing $A$. The line perpendicular to $AD$ through $B$ meets the line parallel to $AD$ through $C$ at the point $E$. The line parallel to $AB$ through $E$ meets $AC$ at the point $F$.

Prove that the angle $\angle AFD$ is a right angle.

A set $S$ of positive integers is called spaced if it contains no pair of elements whose difference is one of the numbers $5, 10, 12, 17$. For example, $\{1, 2, 3, 10, 30\}$ is spaced, while $\{1, 2, 3, 11\}$ is not (because $11 - 1 = 10$). At most how many elements can a spaced subset of $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, 2025, 2026\}$ have?

The band "Mostly Harmless" consists of nine musicians marching in single file. Initially, the distance between each musician and the next one is one metre. At each beat of the bass drum, the first in the line advances one metre. Then, proceeding in order from the second to the eighth, each musician moves to the midpoint between the position occupied by the one ahead of him and the position occupied by the one behind him. Finally, the ninth and last moves to one metre behind the eighth. Decide whether, after a sufficient number of drum beats, the line will exceed $42$ m in length.
